newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-VNU MOVE ENLIVENS BLENHEIM BID SAGA.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-VNU MOVE ENLIVENS BLENHEIM BID SAGA.

text.p: Dutch publisher VNU's decision to take a 15 percent stake in Blenheim Group Plc should force any potential suitors for the British exhibitions organiser to act a little quicker, say analysts.
VNU's share purchase on Tuesday enlivened what had been long running talks rumoured to be between Blenheim and Reed-Elsevier and also United News & Media .
"The ball's very much in Reed's court given they are the ones that have been doing most of the running in talks with Blenheim," said Anthony de Larrinaga at Panmure Gordon.
"The longer Reed doesn't do anything the more likely it is that VNU will come back into the market and acquire more stock." said de Larrinaga, a media analyst at Panmure.

VNU bought the Blenheim shares from institutional shareholders at a price of 500 pence per share, well above the 480p Reed-Elsevier and 450p United News are rumoured to have been discussing with Blenheim, said dealers.
"Immediately it would look rather unlikely that they would be prepared to top 500. But this is a poker game and who knows what will happen," said Nick Ward, a media analyst at Credit Lyonnais Laing.

Of the two, Reed is thought more likely to bite the bullet and launch a bid given the fact that television and newspaper group United News & Media's merged with MAI earlier this year and is seen more likely to make disposals than acquisitions.

"The question now for Reed is whether VNU's entry stimulates it to bigger or better things or whether the thought of VNU as a recalcitrant minority shareholder might put them off," said de Larringa at Panmure.
For its part, VNU has called the move a strategic long term investment and said it had no current intention of making an offer for Blenheim, barring rival offers for the firm.

"A significant investment in such an exhibitions business is...in line with our long-term strategy of expanding in professional information markets," VNU chairman Joep Brentjens said on Tuesday in a statement.

Analysts noted that if the VNU stake purchase were to deter other suitors then the field would be left open for the Dutch publisher to build its stake up to 29.9 percent, at which point a mandatory bid is triggered.
"If they went and offered 470 at the moment I'm sure they would get plenty of stock," said one senior dealer. By 1300 GMT, Blenheim shares were at 462-1/2, down 1-1/2 from Tuesday.

Under takeover rules, however, if the company were to make a formal bid it would have to be pitched at or above the price it paid for any stake of 10 percent and above. In VNU's case 500p, which would value Blenheim at over 450 million sterling.
On the other side of the equation, were Blenheim to recommend an offer from one of the other parties, analysts doubt VNU would want to be left as a minority 15 percent shareholder.
Moreover, analysts agree that to derive the full benefits of Blenheim a full integration of its business would be needed.
"In the fullness of time either VNU or another party is likely to bid, but the likelihood of United, in particular, coming in and topping VNU is not that great," said Ward.
